title: Around the World Stickhandling
description: Full 360-degree puck control drill using a ball or puck. Builds comfort handling the puck in every area around your body while improving mobility and hand speed.
whatYouNeed: A golf ball (recommended) or a puck
dos: Stand in a good hockey stance — feet shoulder-width, chest up, knees bent
Use a golf ball to get comfortable feeling the puck on the blade
Cup the ball on the heel, just like in Quick Hands Warm Up
Start the ball in front of you and take it all the way around your body
Keep your feet still and facing forward — don't step into it
Use your top hand to rotate over and cup the ball — smooth, not choppy
Keep the ball flat on the blade — no popping up in the air
Once you find the rhythm, pick your head up and look forward on both sides
Gradually speed up — aim for smoother and quicker hands over time
donts: Don't stare at the ball the whole time — keep your eyes up and scan forward
Don't move your feet — stay planted and facing forward throughout
Don't hunch over — stay tall with chest up
Don't chop at the ball with your bottom hand — use the top hand to rotate and cup
Don't let the ball pop up in the air — it should stay flat on the blade

title: Quick Hands Warm Up
description: Warm up your hands and build rhythm. Alternating side-to-side puck control through a stickhandling device with a focus on cupping the puck and keeping your eyes up.
whatYouNeed: A stickhandling device (or a row of pucks/cones spaced 6-8 inches apart)
dos: Keep the stickhandling device centered between your feet
Get in a good hockey stance — feet wide, chest up, not too tall and not hunched over
Let the toe of the blade come up off the ice — the heel should make contact, not the middle of the blade
Keep the puck on the heel of the blade, not the middle
Focus on cupping the puck with each touch — dribble twice, cup it, keep it on the heel
Slide the puck under the device and repeat the same motion on the other side
Lower your top hand enough so the toe can lift naturally
Once you find the rhythm, pick your head up and keep it up
Speed it up gradually while maintaining control
donts: Don't stand too tall or hunch over — stay in your hockey stance
Don't stare at the puck — train your hands to feel it while your eyes scan
Don't let the puck sit in the middle of the blade — keep it on the heel
Don't keep the blade flat on the ice — the toe should be up

title: Top Hand Only Stickhandling
description: Forearm strength and puck control drill using only your top hand. Builds the hand strength and blade feel needed for one-handed puck protection and quicker releases.
whatYouNeed: A heavier puck (orange recommended), or a black puck for younger players
dos: Keep the puck on the heel of the blade and cup it with each touch
Maintain a good hockey stance — don't let your posture slip just because you're using one hand
Start with 5 reps or until you feel the forearm burn, then switch to the other side
Push yourself — when the forearm gets tired, grab a black puck and go faster
Work the backhand side too — you need to handle the puck on every part of your body
Take a break, shake it out, then hit the next variation
donts: Don't use your bottom hand — this drill is strictly one-handed
Don't let the blade go flat — keep the puck on the heel at all times

title: Toe Drag Progression
description: Simple toe drag drill working through a line of pucks. Focus on keeping a loose bottom hand and dragging the puck with the toe, not just swiping at it.
whatYouNeed: A line of pucks spaced a few feet apart
dos: Keep your bottom hand loose — don't grip tight
Push the puck out wide with hands close together, then pull it in with the toe
Position your body completely to the right side of the pucks, not in the middle
Exaggerate the toe drag — really grab it with the toe and pull it in
Let your feet and hands move together through the line
It's okay to look at the puck — just never be so hunched over you're vulnerable
donts: Don't keep your feet centered between the pucks — stay to the side
Don't just swipe at the puck — actually drag it with the toe
Don't get caught in a vulnerable hunched position

title: Alternating Circles
description: Alternating toe drag and circle pattern through a line of pucks. Toe drag around one puck, come through the middle, circle around the next — repeat.
whatYouNeed: A line of pucks (5-10, adjust for your space)
dos: Keep your feet wide and the pucks centered between them
Lead with a toe drag around the first puck
Come through the middle, then circle around the next puck
Alternate all the way down — drag, circle, drag, circle
Keep your chest up — it's okay to look at the pucks
Don't worry if you mess up, just keep going
Once you know the pattern, build speed
donts: Don't hunch over — stay in your athletic stance

title: Alternating Circles — Bottom Hand Slide
description: Same alternating circle pattern with emphasis on letting the bottom hand slide. Don't grip too tight — smoothness comes from the top hand leading and the bottom hand adjusting.
whatYouNeed: A line of pucks (5-10 pucks)
dos: Let your bottom hand slide — don't grip it tight
Use your top hand to lead the motion
Start with a toe drag around the first puck
Come through the middle and circle around the next puck
Do 6-8 reps — one rep is going down and back
Once you have the pattern, start building speed
donts: Don't squeeze the bottom hand — stiffness kills control
Don't hunch over when reaching for the far puck — stay tall and reach with your hands
In a game, a hunched position leaves you vulnerable to hits

title: Reverse Alternating Circles
description: Opposite pattern of the alternating circles drill. Start with a circle on the puck closest to your feet, then a toe drag on the far puck — reverse the sequence.
whatYouNeed: A line of pucks (5-10)
dos: Start with a circle on the puck closest to your feet
Come through the middle and do a toe drag on the far puck
Alternate — circle, toe drag, pull through, and repeat
Keep your feet wide, pucks centered between them
Let that bottom hand move — the top hand does most of the work
Do 6-8 reps, 2-3 sets
Once comfortable, snap the toe drag and snap the circle
donts: Don't hunch over — stay in your stance

title: Head Up Stickhandling
description: Build the habit of keeping your head up while stickhandling. Pick two targets in your garage and scan back and forth between them as you handle the puck.
whatYouNeed: Two tape marks or objects across your garage
dos: Pick two spots in your garage — one left, one right
Stickhandle while moving your head side to side between them
Keep your eyes moving as fast as possible from target to target
Challenge yourself by taking quick peeks behind you too
Train this at the end of your stickhandling session after complex drills
donts: Don't stare at the puck — the whole point of this drill is keeping your eyes up

title: One-Leg Balance Stickhandling
description: Balance and puck control drill on one leg. Hockey is played on one leg — train your stability and puck skills at the same time.
whatYouNeed: A puck
dos: Stand on one leg for 30 seconds, then switch to the other leg
Keep your chest up and eyes forward — don't fold over
Maintain a good hockey stance even on one leg
Scan your surroundings as you balance — challenge your stability
Once you're good at it, move the puck to different areas while balancing
donts: Don't let your chest fold over — stay tall
Don't stare down at the puck

title: One-Leg Squat Stickhandling
description: Combine a one-leg squat with stickhandling. Builds leg strength, balance, and puck control all at once — hockey is played on one leg.
whatYouNeed: A puck
dos: Stand on one leg just like the balance drill, but add a squat
Keep your chest and eyes up — don't leave yourself vulnerable
Keep the puck on the heel and cup it each time
Do 5 squats on one leg, switch to the other leg for 5
Complete 2 full sets
donts: Don't hunch over or look down
Don't rush the squat — controlled movement builds real strength

title: Through the Legs Stickhandling
description: Pull the puck behind you and through your legs. Builds comfort handling the puck in every position — expands on the around the world foundation.
whatYouNeed: A puck
dos: Start stationary — 2-3 sets of 10 reps with chest up and good stance
Pull the puck back behind you, keep it on the toe
Let the bottom hand slide through — that's what makes it smooth
It's okay to glance at the puck, especially when learning
Once comfortable, start walking with it — simulate game motion
Progress to receiving bad passes behind you and pulling through
donts: Don't grip too tight — let the bottom hand slide naturally
Don't keep your head locked down — one peek is enough, then eyes up

title: Backhand Toe Drag
description: Deke move dragging the puck from forehand to backhand using the backhand toe. A one-on-one move that also fakes like you're going to shoot.
whatYouNeed: A puck
dos: Start stationary — isolate the backhand toe drag movement
Push the puck forward and drag it back with the back of the toe
The puck should travel on a diagonal, not in an arc
Use your top hand to lead — the bottom hand should not dominate
Once comfortable stationary, add motion
Tape on your blade helps with this move
donts: Don't use the middle of the blade — the name says toe drag for a reason
Don't depend on your bottom hand — keep it loose
Don't swing the puck in an arc — it should glide forward on a diagonal

title: Toe Drag & Soft Chip
description: Toe drag the puck into your feet, then soft chip over a stick. Advanced drill — master the basic fundamentals before attempting this one.
whatYouNeed: A broken stick (or any stick-like object about 2 feet long), pucks, a net
dos: Start with a toe drag, bringing the puck toward your feet
Keep the puck in the middle of your feet as you drag it in
Keep your feet wide — maintain your base
Use your top hand to lead and let the bottom hand slide
Do 5 reps per set, 3 sets total
If you make a mistake, slow it down first, then speed up
donts: Don't try this before mastering basic stickhandling first
Don't stand too straight or narrow — you lose your base
Don't worry about mistakes — it's training, not a game. Keep pushing
notes: Mistakes are part of the process. Same as missing a shot in a game — next rep, next shot. Keep going.

title: Backhand Wand
description: Backhand wand deke — tap the puck on the backhand, let it roll, wand around it, and pull it the other way. Great one-on-one move for defensemen rushing the ice.
whatYouNeed: A puck
dos: Start stationary — get comfortable with the wand motion before adding speed
Tap the puck on the backhand and let it slide in one direction
The wand should happen as the puck is sliding — don't wait too long
Incorporate your whole body — shoulders, head, eyes into the fake
After the wand, extend your hands wide and go the other way
Once comfortable stationary, add motion — skating into the move
donts: Don't wait too long — the wand should come right as the puck starts sliding, not after it's fully there
Don't just move your stick — use your whole body to sell the fake
Don't look awkward — if you're hesitating, slow it down and get the feel first

title: Forehand Wand
description: Forehand version of the wand deke. Push the puck one way, sell the fake with your body, and wand it around to go the other way.
whatYouNeed: A puck
dos: Start stationary — 10-20 reps focusing on the wand motion
Push the puck as if going one way, shift your body the same direction
Wand around the puck and go the opposite way
Use your shoulders, head, and eyes — sell the fake
Once stationary feels smooth, add motion while traveling up the ice
Experiment with using this move on goalies too, not just players
donts: Don't do the wand too early or too late — time it as the puck slides
Don't just do a basic forehand-to-backhand move — the wand should be distinct
Don't slide the puck all the way before starting the move

title: Foundation Snap Shot
description: The perfect drill for dialing in your snap shot and correcting form. If your mechanics are off, you won't be able to get power on this shot — the drill forces you to place the puck in the right position and take a compact, proper snap. Great for developing players learning to generate power and confidence in their release. The drill exaggerates the push-puck-away-then-pop technique that's essential to every snap shot.
whatYouNeed: A net, pucks
dos: Drag the puck to a spot where you can one-touch it
Let your hips and body rotate toward the net
Use a staggered stance — copy the footwork shown in the video
Focus specifically on being compact and efficient with every movement
donts: Don't try to overpower it — if your form is off, the shot won't work, so let the drill correct your mechanics
Don't reach for the puck — bring it into your body before releasing
Don't rush the push-pop sequence — it should be one fluid motion
notes: Kids and developing players benefit most from this. The push-puck-away technique gets exaggerated naturally, which is exactly what builds a proper snap shot foundation.

title: Explosive Pop Snap
description: Train a quicker, more explosive snap that transfers to every shot type.
whatYouNeed: Two broken sticks, 1-3 feet gap between them
dos: Focus solely on the snap
Keep your body relaxed
Pop the puck from the toe of the blade as quick as you can
donts: Don't drag the puck and turn it into a Bedard style shot
You should solely be focusing on the snap release
Don't need to move your feet — body should stay relaxed
notes: Work on this — you should be able to eventually get power on the shot even in this small surface area. Don't worry if it's lighter at first, keep working!

title: Snapshots on Passer
description: Snapshot off the top of the passer in a limited surface area. Trains you to generate power off the end of your release, building a quicker, more compact snap that's less predictable and highly effective in close quarters. The power transfers to every other shot — even when you're further out and drag the puck for a windup, you still snap and pop at the end.
whatYouNeed: A passer (or helper), a net, pucks
dos: Keep your top hand up high near your chest
Let your hand punch out slightly, then snap back quickly — that's where the pop and spin comes from
Keep your feet still, body relaxed
Watch the demonstration closely and mirror the mechanics
donts: Don't drag the puck into a toe drag release — this drill is pure snap, no angle change needed
Don't stare down at the puck the whole time
Don't pull your stick back and slap at the puck
Don't stress if you're not getting power at first — this takes time to master and pays off long-term for your release
notes: The second video is a slowed-down version without gloves so you can observe the hand mechanics more closely. Both videos show the same drill.

title: Toe Drag Release
description: Toe drag to release into a powerful shot. Build up to it.
whatYouNeed: A cone (or puck, bucket, chair with a stick)
dos: Hips rotate toward net, feet stay mostly planted
Start easy, feet not too close to the cone
Drag the puck with the toe, get a powerful pop off release
Elbow up, allow the sling push-pull motion
As you improve, move your feet closer to the cone — release the puck between your feet with weight on top of the puck for flex and power
donts: Don't step away from the cone before the release
Don't look down at the puck the whole time

title: Finding Shooting Lanes
description: Change the angle, find the lane. Use a Bedard-style release and forehand-backhand fakes to create space and open up scoring areas.
whatYouNeed: A cone (or bucket/chair), a net, pucks
dos: Let your body flow naturally — be involved in the fake before the shot
Be intentional about where you aim — shoot for practical scoring areas
Remember spots on the net where you've scored in games — aim for those areas
donts: Don't just step to the side and shoot — the Bedard pull needs to bring the puck toward your feet
Don't make the fake with just your stick — use your whole body

title: Catch & Release Shot
description: Game-like catch and release shot. Train receiving a pass and getting the shot off quickly with your head up — simulates in-game timing.
whatYouNeed: A passer (or a helper), a pile of pucks, a net
dos: Receive the puck and get the shot off quickly
Pick a spot, hit it a few times before switching targets
Keep your head up — scan the net before the shot comes off
Lefties: go low blocker. Righties: go low glove
Build the habit of seeing what the goalie is giving you
donts: Don't look down for a long time — eyes should be scanning the net before you release

title: High Slot One-Timer
description: High slot one-timer drill. Train reading the pass, picking your spot, and snapping it off quick from the slot — simulates the most dangerous scoring area on the ice.
whatYouNeed: A passer (or helper), a pile of pucks, a net
dos: Lefties: shoot top right (right side of net) — where the goalie is sliding toward
Righties: shoot top left (opposite corner)
On a slow pass, go across the grain
Hit five in one spot before moving to the next target
Snap it quick — high slot windows close fast
donts: Don't raise your stick above your head like a slap shot
This is a high slot one-timer, not a blue line bomb — keep the stick lower and snap through the puck

title: In Tight Finishing
description: In tight finishing drill. Quick feet, soft hands, one-touch chip shots around the net — everything happens fast in tight.
whatYouNeed: A net, pucks
dos: Keep feet planted, facing the net
Quick dribble stickhandle with body movement on the fake
Focus on chipping the puck up high
Make it a one-touch chip shot — quick and soft
donts: Don't move your feet
Don't do a long wrist shot
Don't fully rotate your body and do a slow long backhander

title: Slide Under & Release
description: Slide the puck under a defender's stick and get a quick one-touch release off. Simulates the tight-space shot you need when a defenseman closes the gap on you.
whatYouNeed: A stickhandler device, bucket with a stick, or a chair with a stick — something to slide under
dos: Come in wide like you're attacking the defenseman
Slide the puck under the stick as the defender reaches/pokes
Get into position and snap a quick release
Choose your spot — short side, far side, over the pad
Practice getting shots off with the puck in different positions around your feet
Lefties: short side bar down is a great option. Over the pad too
donts: Don't try to go to the other side of the stick — the move is sliding under, not around
Don't wind up big — this is a quick release drill, not a slap shot

title: One-Legged Chair Shots
description: Practice your one-legged in-stride shot by putting your back foot on a chair. Hockey is played off one leg — this builds the strength and comfort to shoot off either leg in game situations.
whatYouNeed: A sturdy chair, a net, pucks
dos: Place your back foot on a chair, fully extend the shooting leg
Keep your head up looking at the net
Get your top arm out and elbow up — punch through the shot
Lefties: shooting off the left leg, right leg on the chair
Righties: shooting off the right leg, left leg on the chair
Do about 30 pucks — you should feel it in your glute
Even if you already know one-legged shots, this builds strength
donts: Don't stand too close to the chair — extend out like you would in a game
Don't drop your head — keep your eyes on the target
Don't rush into this before mastering the basic snap shot

title: One-Legged Shot In Stride
description: Learn to take a one-legged shot in motion. Start with a step-over landing on your shooting leg, then add the puck — simulates receiving a pass and shooting off one leg in a game.
whatYouNeed: A broken stick (optional), a net, pucks
dos: Start with right foot in front of left (lefties) — take a step and land on your left leg
Do this 10 times without the puck — get used to the weight transfer
Add your stick and body — look at the net as you land
Once the transfer feels natural, add the puck — snap it as you land
Righties: left foot in front of right, land on right leg
If you already know one-legged shots, practice from different areas of your garage to simulate game spots
donts: Don't try this before you're comfortable with the stationary chair shot first
Don't overcomplicate it — the motion is just a step and a land
